## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

1. **A handler that dies on the poison message (panic/OOM) rather than returning an error.** `Settle` is the only entry point to the library's dispositions — ladder, exhaustion, and breaker alike — so such a message is not settled by *any* of them, under any trigger design; this is a property of the callback contract, not of the elapsed-time clock. **Detection is unaffected:** FloorMonitor polls independently of message flow and keeps reporting the stall for as long as the process lives; the ack-floor monitor still pages; a crash-looping pod is its own alerting surface. **Remediation is deliberately not attempted:** recovering the panic in `Process` to Ack/dead-letter the message is rejected as contrary to the module's fatal-panic posture (`nuts.ShutdownGroup` recovers a panicking loop only to drain, then treats it as fatal to the group — "so a dead consumer cannot leave its process looking healthy"). The upper bound against the stall SLA stays the adopter's arithmetic (`FloorAge + largest rung + AckWait`) — the library cannot know the SLA.
3. **Selectivity under mass failure:** at most **one claimed message per stall window**, window resets only when the ack floor *moves* — successive floor-holders drain back-to-back, a claim that didn't move the floor waits out a full window, and a false positive is bounded to one message per FloorAge. 4. **Trigger behind an internal `stallSignal` interface** (FloorMonitor separate from Retry) — a future native MaxPendingAge-style server trigger slots in without touching the capture-then-Ack path.
5. **`BreakerObserve` consumes the same one-per-stall-window budget as enforcing** — observe mode is a faithful dry run: the trip counts a soak collects are exactly what enforce would produce, not the far larger number of messages that merely satisfied the conditions. Shortening the ladder is right *per consumer* and already shipped for entire-search (#173: MaxDeliver 5, ~43 min — why the pages stopped). The breaker solves what a ladder cannot:

1. **A ladder can't tell poison from transient — floor-holding time can.** The ack floor is a watermark: it only moves when the *oldest unacked* message settles, so every failing message eventually holds it. The discriminator is **for how long**: transients hold the floor for minutes (everything that recovered on Aug 6 did so by attempt 3–4, ≤ ~10 min of cumulative floor-holding); poison holds it until exhaustion or manual removal (measured: 10h20m on Aug 6; 34h22m under the pre-fix ladder). A floor-stationary-age trigger at 15–20 min therefore never fires on a transient and always catches poison — and it identifies exactly which message to dead-letter (the one at the floor). A short ladder instead dead-letters *every* failure fast, including the ones that would have recovered, onto DLQs whose replay is manual.
2. **Ladders lie.** The Session-1 forensics proved entire-search's configured ladder was dead config for weeks (NakWithDelay override + server BackOff-stretch): "17h45m" was 34h22m in reality. A ladder-based safety property trusts config; the breaker measures observed state and holds even when the retry schedule is wrong — which is the failure mode we actually had.
3. **Per-consumer ladder tuning is the whack-a-mole.** #173 fixed one durable; every other hand-rolled consumer has its own schedule, and nothing stops the next 34-hour one. The breaker in `jsconsumer` + Track D migration makes "no message holds the floor > threshold" a fleet invariant written once.

Why a stuck floor matters even while later messages keep processing out of order: the pinned message burns a worker slot every redelivery; the stall monitor can't distinguish one pinned message from real throughput collapse (that ambiguity was the 12 auto-P1s); and on a limits stream, a message still unacked at maxAge is reaped silently — the exact mechanism of the Jul 31–Aug 4 data loss (ENT-1492).

Ladders stay tunable per workload; the breaker is the backstop underneath. content.content:
acknowledgement *timeouts*, so a plain `Nak` asks for immediate redelivery
  and skips the ladder entirely (measured against a live server: 0s versus the
  configured rung). A consumer that Naks burns `MaxDeliver` in milliseconds.

  That split is the ENT-1535 finding, not a detail. A JetStream consumer has
  two possible redelivery schedulers, and setting both does not pick one: the
  server stretches each client `NakWithDelay` by the BackOff increments, so
  redeliveries follow neither and the configured ladder becomes dead config
  that still reads as authoritative — a consumer advertising 17h45m while
  really taking 34h22m, with nothing saying so. Exactly one scheduler is what
  prevents that, and the one that composes with declarative fleet management is
  the server's. `RetryConfig` has no ladder fields, so nothing you configure
  *here* can produce a second scheduler.

  That is narrower than it sounds, and worth stating as an adoption contract
  rather than a guarantee: a handler still holds the `jetstream.Msg` and can
  call `NakWithDelay` itself, and `backoff.Policy` is still exported for
  callers that predate this package. Either recreates the exact defect
  alongside a server ladder. What the library can promise is that `Settle` is
  the whole disposition it owns, and that `Schedule` flags the combination
  wherever a config is modelled — including configs the library would never
  construct. Handlers that Nak on their own are outside that.

  Bound that ladder with `MaxTimeToDeadLetter` and it is the whole remedy: a
  poison message reaches capture-then-Ack inside the SLA with no inference
  about which message is at fault. This is what a consumer should adopt today.
  Two things about that ladder that are easy to get wrong, and that `Schedule`
  models so the bound is checked against what actually runs: the server repeats
  the last `backOff` entry once the array runs out, so a short list is not a
  short ladder; and an *absent* `backOff` is not an absent ladder — the broker
  redelivers on `AckWait`, so the effective schedule becomes AckWait repeated
  up to `MaxDeliver`.

  Never a drop, and never a bare `Term` — the objection to `Term` being the
  missing record, not the settlement: measured against nats-server 2.14.3 it
  settles cleanly on limits, workqueue and interest alike, it just leaves no
  trace of what was discarded. A failed capture leaves the message
  for the server to redeliver, so it survives and the stall stays visible — and `CaptureReserve` holds
  back deliveries specifically to retry it. When even those are spent the
  message is reported as `OutcomeStranded`, not dressed up as a retry: at the
  delivery cap nothing redelivers, so nothing will touch it again and it needs
  the break-glass runbook. Alert on that outcome.

  **Explicit non-goal:** a handler that *dies* on the poison message — panics,
  OOMs — rather than returning an error. `Settle` is the only entry point to
  every disposition the package owns, so such a message is not settled by any
  of them; that follows from the callback contract, not from the breaker.
  Recovering the panic to Ack the message would hide the bug and leave the
  handler's state unreconciled, against the module's existing posture that a
  panicking loop is fatal (`ShutdownGroup`). The stall stays loud — the
  monitor polls independently of message flow and the ack-floor monitor still
  pages — it just isn't auto-remediated.
- **`jsconsumer.FloorMonitor`** — the durable's ack-floor health signal, and
  the telemetry half of the poison-message story: it polls the floor and
  reports how long it has been *stalled*, which is the signal the ack-floor
  monitor pages on, available in-process rather than by polling consumer info
  a second time. `Start` polls it and `Stop` joins the poll. Use it for a
  gauge and an alert; that is its supported role.

  It measures **floor-stall age**, not message stream-age: the two diverge
  badly under backlog, where 35 minutes of receipt→first-delivery lag on a
  perfectly healthy message would read as a stall. Stalled is also not the
  same as *stationary* — the clock runs only while the consumer has delivered
  past its own floor, so an idle consumer's motionless floor never accrues
  time to charge the next arriving message with.

  **The circuit breaker built on it is experimental.** Attaching the monitor to
  `RetryConfig.Monitor` lets `Retry` evaluate whether a stalled floor plus a
  message that has itself been failing that long warrants quarantining it —
  but `Breaker`'s zero value is `BreakerObserve`, which measures without

jsconsumer: correct beliefs the broker-semantics suite measured differently

COR-1257's suite contradicted three things this package asserted. Verified the
load-bearing one here rather than taking it on report, and it holds.

TERM SETTLES. Measured on nats-server 2.14.3 single-node across limits,
workqueue and interest retention: after a Term the ack floor advances past the
message and NumAckPending returns to zero, and on workqueue/interest the
message also leaves the stream. ENT-1492's write-up implies otherwise and this
package repeated it. The objection to a bare Term is the missing RECORD, not
the settlement, and that is the only part the capture-first design ever
depended on — so no behaviour changes, but the reasoning no longer teaches
something false to whoever reads it next. (The production wedge ENT-1492
recorded is better explained by the COR-1224 ack-permission gap: acks are
fire-and-forget publishes to $JS.ACK.>, so without publish rights msg.Ack()
returns nil while the floor stays pinned. That is precisely why the terminal
path here uses DoubleAck.)

NAKWITHDELAY CANNOT EXPRESS ITS OWN ENVELOPE. The server backdates the pending
timestamp by AckWait and measures it against the CURRENT rung, so the effective
wait is d + (BackOff[rung] - BackOff[0]). Measured on [200ms, 1200ms],
NakWithDelay(50ms) redelivered at 50ms, 1050ms, 1050ms. My own 3s/3s/3s
measurement could not see this because a flat ladder's stretch is zero. This
makes the case for doing nothing stronger than the one previously documented:
not merely that a client would have to know the delay, but that on a growing
ladder its timing is not predictable at all. Also the likeliest explanation for
ENT-1535's unverified "~78s against a 5m first rung".

FLOOR+1 FLIPS ON AN UNRELATED ACK. The failure is narrower and stranger than
"after a drain": with unmatched sequences below the blocker and nothing acked
beneath them the floor sits under those, so floor+1 names a message the
consumer never receives — and one ack of any matching message below the
blocker makes the floor skip the unmatched run so floor+1 starts naming the
blocker correctly. Stream-side removal drags the floor to the delivered
high-water mark with no ack at all. Rewritten to describe the mechanism rather
than a figure another session could not reproduce.

Two confirmations folded in where they matter: an exhausted message pins the
floor with NumAckPending at ZERO, which is direct evidence for the
delivered-versus-floor stall gate over the num-ack-pending one the monitor text
suggests; and a stream's ConsumerLimits silently fill an unset
InactiveThreshold, so a consumer can inherit a deletion timer it never asked
for — noted on the field.

Refs ENT-1601, ENT-1535, ENT-1492, COR-1257, COR-1224.

13	// dlqPublishTimeout bounds one dead-letter PublishMsg. The consume context has
14	// no deadline, and PublishMsg waits for the PubAck indefinitely; without a
15	// bound a NATS blip would hang the handler (and, since a one-in-flight consumer
16	// keeps a slot occupied, stall the consumer) instead of failing the capture
17	// loudly.
18	const dlqPublishTimeout = 15 * time.Second
19	
20	// DLQ provenance headers added to the captured copy so a replay tool (or a
21	// human) can see why and from where a message was dead-lettered.
22	const (
23		DLQReasonHeader    = "Nats-Dlq-Reason"
24		DLQOriginHeader    = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Subject"
25		DLQDeliveredHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Delivered"
26		DLQStreamSeqHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Stream-Seq"
27	)
28	
29	// DLQPublisher is the publish surface DeadLetter needs — the modern
30	// [JetStream] publish primitive (satisfied by jetstream.JetStream), aliased
31	// so DeadLetter's signature reads in DLQ terms. Kept minimal so wiring can
32	// hand it the same JetStream handle the per-cell publishers already hold,
33	// and tests can stub it.
34	type DLQPublisher = JetStream
35	
36	// SubjectToken sanitizes s into a single valid NATS subject token. NATS tokens
37	// cannot contain spaces, dots, or wildcards, so every character outside
38	// [a-z0-9_-] is replaced with '_' (and letters are lowercased). Use it to turn a
39	// human-readable dead-letter reason ("bad completion payload") into a subject
40	// token ("bad_completion_payload") — publishing to an unsanitized reason would
41	// fail, so the caller would never Ack the poison off a WorkQueue.
42	func SubjectToken(s string) string {
43		// Iterate bytes, not runes: we only keep ASCII [a-z0-9_-] and map everything
44		// else (including every byte of a multi-byte rune) to '_', so a byte loop is
45		// both correct and free of a rune->byte narrowing conversion.
46		b := make([]byte, 0, len(s))
47		for i := range len(s) {
48			c := s[i]
49			switch {
50			case c >= 'a' && c <= 'z', c >= '0' && c <= '9', c == '_', c == '-':
51				b = append(b, c)
52			case c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z':
53				b = append(b, c-'A'+'a')
54			default:
55				b = append(b, '_')
56			}
57		}
58		if len(b) == 0 {
59			return "unknown"
60		}
61		return string(b)
62	}
63	
64	// DeadLetter republishes a poison message to dlqSubject, preserving its payload
65	// and headers and adding Nats-Dlq-* provenance (reason, origin subject,
66	// delivery count, stream sequence).
67	//
68	// It is the capture step a consumer runs before giving up on a message it can
69	// never process. DeadLetter copies the poison to a durable DLQ subject so it can
70	// be inspected or replayed, and the caller then removes the original from the
71	// stream — a Term on the final delivery (see backoff.Policy.TermOnExhaustion,
72	// whose doc notes callers "DLQ capture before calling NakOrTerm") or a plain
73	// Ack. Without this step a Term'd or MaxDeliver-exhausted message is discarded
74	// with no trail; DeadLetter is what makes the give-up auditable and recoverable.
75	//
76	// Returns an error if the republish fails; on error the caller MUST NOT remove
77	// the original — Nak or leave it so the poison is never dropped without a
78	// captured copy. Publishing is bounded by dlqPublishTimeout regardless of ctx's
79	// deadline.
80	func DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, pub DLQPublisher, dlqSubject string, msg jetstream.Msg, reason string) error {
81		hdr := nats.Header{}
82		for k, v := range msg.Headers() {
83			hdr[k] = append([]string(nil), v...)
84		}
85		hdr.Set(DLQReasonHeader, reason)
86		hdr.Set(DLQOriginHeader, msg.Subject())
87		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
88			hdr.Set(DLQDeliveredHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.NumDelivered, 10))
89			hdr.Set(DLQStreamSeqHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.Sequence.Stream, 10))
90		}
91	
92		out := &nats.Msg{Subject: dlqSubject, Data: msg.Data(), Header: hdr}
93	
94		pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)
95		defer cancel()
96		if _, err := pub.PublishMsg(pubCtx, out); err != nil {
97			return fmt.Errorf("dead-letter publish to %q: %w", dlqSubject, err)
98		}
99		return nil
100	}

timing, on a message the broker would have accepted, and OutcomeStranded is
precisely the outcome that means "a human must run the break-glass runbook".

a responder at a message that needed one more round-trip. Both are the same
defect: nothing about the terminal path wants to be abandoned halfway, and it is
the only path where giving up costs a pinned floor.

unchanged and are what keep this safe: the capture publish and the DoubleAck
each apply their own timeout (dlqPublishTimeout, dlqAckTimeout), which matters
because WithoutCancel drops the parent's deadline along with its cancellation.

the capture. This narrows the window rather than closing it absolutely — a
terminate outlasting nuts.DefaultJoinTimeout still has its connection drained
under it — but it removes the case that failed immediately and by construction.

discards the one it is handed and fakeDLQ ignores it, so a cancellation test
written against them would pass on the unfixed code. Two local doubles fix that
